# On the Strange Comfort of Incomplete Things

There's a mug on my desk that's missing its handle. It sits there among the functional ceramics, and I've never thrown it away, though I've had plenty of opportunities. Every time I clean, I pick it up, consider it, and then return it to its spot. I think there's something worth examining in that impulse—the strange reluctance we feel to discard imperfect objects.

Most of us are raised with a kind of implicit perfectionism. Things should work. Objects should serve their purposes. A mug without a handle has failed at its primary job, which is to be held comfortably while containing hot liquid. Yet I keep it. Why? Because I find myself drawn to what it represents—a narrative of use, of time passing, of something that was whole once and now isn't, but still exists. It's archaeological in a way. It's a small monument to the fact that nothing lasts unchanged.

I think about this a lot lately—how much of our anxiety comes from the expectation that things should be intact, that we should be intact. We speak about our mental health in terms of being "broken" or needing to be "fixed," as though wholeness is the natural state and fracture is an aberration. But is it? Walk through any old city and you'll see buildings that have been patched and modified countless times, that bear the marks of centuries, and somehow they're more beautiful for it. The kintsugi tradition in Japanese ceramics goes even further—it glorifies the repair, making the breaks visible with gold, transforming damage into decoration.

I wonder what would change if we approached our own incompleteness this way. Not as failures to achieve some imagined perfect state, but as evidence of having been alive, of having weathered something.

There's also something liberating about incomplete things, I think. A finished project can be intimidating. You judge it against some ideal. But an incomplete thing—well, it still has possibilities. That half-written story on your computer could become anything. The half-finished painting leans against the wall, waiting for you to discover what it actually wants to be. There's hope in incompletion that perfection paradoxically destroys. Once something is complete, it can only degrade or be judged. While it remains unfinished, it remains full of potential.

I've noticed this in conversations too. The best ones never feel finished. You leave them still thinking, still turning over what was said, still discovering new implications days later. The conversations that feel complete, that wrap up neatly with satisfying conclusions, often feel hollow in retrospect. We think we connected, but the other person has already moved on, the moment is sealed shut. But the inconclusive conversation, the one where you both hung in the space of uncertainty together—that one stays with you. It keeps working on you, the way that mug keeps working on me.

This might be why I'm suspicious of self-help books and life advice in general, even as I understand why people seek them out. We want someone to tell us the complete truth, the final answer, the way to fix ourselves. But real growth doesn't work that way. It's messier. It's partial knowledge that you have to keep re-examining. It's taking advice that contradicts other advice you've been given, and somehow learning to live in that contradiction. It's becoming more complicated, not less.

The older I get, the more I notice that the people I most admire are not the ones who seem to have it all figured out. They're the ones who are comfortable admitting what they don't know, who can hold conflicting ideas at once, who haven't stopped asking questions. They've made peace with their incompleteness. There's a kind of grace in that—a refusal to perform certainty that they don't feel.

I think about the books I love most, and so many of them have unsatisfying endings. Or rather, endings that satisfy something deeper than plot resolution—they satisfy the need for honesty. They end where the story actually ends, not where convention suggests stories should end. They leave you with questions. They trust you to do the work of interpretation.

There's a line in one of Elena Ferrante's novels where she writes about how we go through life leaving pieces of ourselves everywhere, in the people we meet, in the experiences we have, and we're never fully present anywhere because we're always partially distributed across all our past encounters. We're incomplete creatures by definition, scattered across time. Maybe the only way to survive that is to stop trying to gather ourselves back together into some coherent whole and instead accept the scattering as our fundamental condition.

I think this is what draws me to reading biographies and essays—they're often more honest about incompletion than fiction is. A life doesn't resolve into a narrative arc unless you impose one on it afterward. The actual living of it is contradictory, unresolved, full of threads that lead nowhere and questions that remain open. We're always in the middle of becoming, never arriving at final definitions of ourselves.

So I keep that mug. And I use other complete mugs for my coffee, because pragmatism is also important. But I keep the broken one because it reminds me of something I need to remember regularly: that damage is not the opposite of value, that incompleteness is not a temporary state to be fixed but a permanent condition to be accepted and even cherished. The cracks are where the light gets in, as Leonard Cohen said, though he was quoting Rumi, because nothing is ever original anyway. Everything is a fragment of something else, all of us composed of broken pieces fitted together, and the coherence we feel is an illusion we maintain together through collective agreement.

Maybe that's the most honest thing I can say: we're all walking around with missing handles, and the secret is learning not to mind, and even learning to find that beautiful.
